items.title: A day after Theni jailbreak, 13 out of 17 escapees apprehended
items.summary: The Tamil Nadu police have arrested 13 among the 17 remand prisoners who escaped from the District Jail at Thekkampatti in Theni district on Monday, October 26. A search is underway for the remaining four escapees. According to the Prison Department's press release issued on Tuesday, October 27, the jailbreak occurred around 10 pm, when some inmates raised an alarm claiming that a prisoner in the third block was experiencing an epileptic seizure. When the Grade II warder on duty in the block, Stalin Prabhu, entered to check on the inmate, the prisoners allegedly attacked him and attempted to escape. They subsequently confronted the guards at the main gate, snatched the keys, and opened the main entrance to flee the premises. According to preliminary reports, all 17 prisoners were lodged in the same cell. The District Jail at Thekkampatti has an authorised capacity of 200 inmates. However, 334 prisoners were housed there at the time of the incident, the Prison Department said in the release. items.title: Musk's outbursts explained: What an Indian licence can do for Starlink
items.summary: Starlink has had its Indian licence since June 2025. As of late October, sixteen months on, it still can’t sell anyone a connection. The latest hold-up, if Bloomberg ’s June report is right, is the Home Ministry, which has been sitting on the final security clearance since Starlink dishes turned up in the Iran war, in a country where Starlink was never licensed. Starlink calls that report misleading and says it has built a deployment model tailored for India . In early October, Elon Musk lost patience in public and blamed Mukesh Ambani . The Narendra Modi government says it is simply following process. While one camp considers Starlink a foreign threat to be kept out, the other thinks every week of delay means villages are kept offline for a tycoon’s benefit. Since the back-and-forth in the public square is bereft of context or nuance, this piece tries to provide that missing link. Its central point is simple: an Indian licence gives India a handle on the parts of Starlink that physically sit in India, but not on the satellites overhead or the software that decides whose dish works.
